kangaroo-at-2023-student-02.title: Try from the top
kangaroo-at-2023-student-02.body:
- Four sixes give 24 > 19 already.
- Three sixes give 18, and the other two dice show at least $1 + 1 = 2$, total at least 20 > 19.
- Two sixes work: $6 + 6 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 19$.

**Answer: (C) 2**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-03.title: Vertical and horizontal parts separately
kangaroo-at-2023-student-03.body:
**Vertical parts.** The ant only ever goes up, and it climbs from the bottom to the top, so the vertical pieces add up to the height: 15 cm.

**Horizontal parts.** All arcs go round the tin in the same direction. Follow the angle: from $A$ the ant goes round to the right-front line (almost one full turn: one turn minus the small front gap between the two front lines), then from there round past the front, past $A$'s line and all the way to the back and on to $B$'s line (one full turn plus that gap). $B$ lies directly above $A$. Altogether the arcs make exactly 2 full turns: $2\cdot 30 = 60$ cm.

Total: $15 + 60 = 75$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 75 cm**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-04.title: No carries
kangaroo-at-2023-student-04.body:
$A\cdot1111 = A\cdot1000 + A\cdot100 + A\cdot10 + A$: four shifted copies of $111\dots1$. Adding them column by column, every column sum is at most 4, so there are no carries: the result is $1234\,44\dots4\,321$. Its digit sum equals the total of all the digits in the four copies: $4\cdot 2023 = 8092$.

**Answer: (D) 8092**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-04.title: Count the digits
kangaroo-at-2023-student-04.body:
The product has $2026$ digits: $1,2,3$, then $2020$ fours, then $3,2,1$. Digit sum: $1+2+3+4\cdot2020+3+2+1 = 12 + 8080 = 8092$.

**Answer: (D) 8092**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-05.title: Strip by strip
kangaroo-at-2023-student-05.body:
Top strip: 4 choices. Middle strip: any colour except the top one, 3 choices. Bottom strip: any colour except the middle one, 3 choices (it may repeat the top colour). Total $4\cdot3\cdot3 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-05.title: Split by top = bottom
kangaroo-at-2023-student-05.body:
Top and bottom the same: $4$ choices for them, $3$ for the middle: 12. Top and bottom different: $4\cdot 3$ choices for them and then $2$ for the middle (different from both): 24. Total $12 + 24 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-06.title: Only 4
kangaroo-at-2023-student-06.body:
A number with exactly three divisors is the square of a prime, $p^2$, with divisors $1, p, p^2$. Here the middle divisor must be 2, so $p=2$ and $n=4$. Exactly one number.

**Answer: (B) 1**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-06.title: Direct
kangaroo-at-2023-student-06.body:
$n$ is divisible by 2, and $\frac n2$ is also a divisor of $n$. It must be one of $1, 2, n$, so $\frac n2 = 1$ or $\frac n2 = 2$. $n=2$ has only the two divisors 1 and 2; $n = 4$ has exactly the divisors 1, 2, 4. ✓ So there is exactly one twoprime number.

**Answer: (B) 1**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-07.title: Last digits
kangaroo-at-2023-student-07.body:
Every power $5^k$ ($k\ge1$) ends in 5, so each factor ends in 6. The product of numbers ending in 6 ends in 6 ($6\cdot6 = 36$, $6\cdot 6 = 36$).

**Answer: (E) 6**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-09.title: Blocks of kangaroos
kangaroo-at-2023-student-09.body:
A kangaroo also needs a kangaroo neighbour, so kangaroos sit in blocks of at least 2. Between two neighbouring blocks there can be at most 2 beavers (a third beaver in the middle would have no kangaroo neighbour), and at each end of the row at most 1 beaver.

With $m$ blocks there are at least $2m$ kangaroos and at most $2(m-1) + 2 = 2m$ beavers. So beavers $\le$ kangaroos, i.e. beavers $\le 11$ (since $23$ is odd, 11.5 is impossible).

11 is possible: $B\,KK\,BB\,KK\,BB\,KK\,BB\,KK\,BB\,KK\,BB\,KK$ — 11 beavers, 12 kangaroos.

**Answer: (D) 11**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-10.title: Geometric series
kangaroo-at-2023-student-10.body:
At each step the black square is $\frac14$ of the current square, and the next square is also $\frac14$ of it. So the black area is
$$84\left(\tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \tfrac1{64}+\dots\right) = 84\cdot\frac{1/4}{1 - 1/4} = 84\cdot\frac13 = 28.$$

**Answer: (B) 28**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-10.title: Symmetry
kangaroo-at-2023-student-10.body:
In each split, the upper-left (black) square and the lower-left and upper-right squares are equally big. Colour the lower-left squares grey and the upper-right squares white; at every stage black, grey and white get the same amount, and together they fill the whole square (the remaining part shrinks to a point). So black is $\frac13$ of 84, which is 28.

**Answer: (B) 28**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-11.title: Residues repeat with period 3
kangaroo-at-2023-student-11.body:
If $x_i + x_{i+1} + x_{i+2}$ and $x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}+x_{i+3}$ are both multiples of 3, then $x_i \equiv x_{i+3} \pmod 3$. So squares 1, 4, 7 have the same remainder mod 3, as do squares 2, 5, 8 and squares 3, 6, 9; the three remainders must be 0, 1, 2 in some order (their sum is a multiple of 3, and each remainder class $\{3,6,9\}, \{1,4,7\}, \{2,5,8\}$ has exactly three numbers).

7 is in square 2, so squares 2, 5, 8 hold $\{1,4,7\}$; 9 is in square 4, so squares 1, 4, 7 hold $\{3,6,9\}$; squares 3, 6, 9 hold $\{2,5,8\}$.

Count: squares 1, 7 get 3 and 6 in $2$ ways; squares 5, 8 get 1 and 4 in $2$ ways; squares 3, 6, 9 get 2, 5, 8 in $3! = 6$ ways. Total $2\cdot2\cdot6 = 24$.

**Answer: (E) 24**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-12.title: Extend to an equilateral triangle
kangaroo-at-2023-student-12.body:
All angles of the hexagon are $120^\circ$. Name the sides in order $6, 15, 11, 12, x, y$ (top, upper right, lower right, bottom, lower left, upper left). Extending every second side of an equiangular hexagon gives an equilateral triangle whose side is the sum of three consecutive hexagon sides: so
$$6 + 15 + 11 = 11 + 12 + x = x + y + 6.$$
From the first equality $x = 9$, from the second $y = 17$. Perimeter: $6+15+11+12+9+17 = 70$.

**Answer: (D) 70**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-12.title: Differences of opposite sides
kangaroo-at-2023-student-12.body:
In a hexagon with all angles $120^\circ$ and sides $a_1,\dots,a_6$ in order, going once round the hexagon as vectors gives $a_1 - a_4 = a_5 - a_2 = a_3 - a_6$ (the sides point in six directions $60^\circ$ apart). With $a_1=6$, $a_2=15$, $a_3=11$, $a_4=12$:
$$6 - 12 = a_5 - 15 = 11 - a_6 \implies a_5 = 9,\ a_6 = 17.$$
Perimeter $= 6+15+11+12+9+17 = 70$.

**Answer: (D) 70**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-14.title: Triangle inequalities
kangaroo-at-2023-student-14.body:
Call the apex $T$, the right vertex $R$ and the bottom vertices $L$ (left) and $M$. The diagram gives $TL = 7$, $TR = 3$, $RM = 4$, $LM = 2$. Unknown: $TM = x$ and $LR = y$ (dashed).
- Face $TLM$ (7, 2, $x$): $5 < x < 9$. Face $TRM$ (3, 4, $x$): $1 < x < 7$. So $x = 6$.
- Face $LMR$ (2, 4, $y$): $2 < y < 6$. Face $TLR$ (7, 3, $y$): $4 < y < 10$. So $y = 5$.

Sum: $6 + 5 = 11$.

**Answer: (C) 11**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-15.title: Parity
kangaroo-at-2023-student-15.body:
$2m - 2023$ is odd, so $|2m-2023| \ge 1$. Hence $|2m - 2023| = 1$ and $|2n - m| = 0$. So $m \in\{1011, 1012\}$ and $m = 2n$ is even: $m = 1012$, $n = 506$. Exactly one pair.

**Answer: (B) 1**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-16.title: Try $n = 5^k$
kangaroo-at-2023-student-16.body:
If $n = 5^k$ then $n^n = 5^{k\cdot5^k}$. We need $k\cdot 5^k = 5^6$, which holds for $k = 5$: $5\cdot5^5 = 5^6$. So $n = 5^5 = 5\cdot5^4$.

**Answer: (A) $5\cdot5^4$**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-17.title: Glue the edges
kangaroo-at-2023-student-17.body:
Fold each net mentally and check the edges that get glued together: wherever the path hits the boundary of the net, it must continue on the face that is glued to that edge, at the matching point; and in the end all pieces must join up into **one** closed loop.

In (A), (B), (C) and (E) at least one path end runs into an edge whose partner edge carries no path at that point (or the pieces close up into more than one loop). In (D) every path end on the boundary meets a path end on the glued edge, and following the path you visit all pieces and come back to the start: a single closed path.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-19.title: Make the $a$-term vanish
kangaroo-at-2023-student-19.body:
$y = x^3 + 3x^2 + 4 + a(x+2)$. The value is independent of $a$ exactly when $x = -2$; then $y = -8 + 12 + 4 = 8$. The common point is $(-2, 8)$ and the sum of its coordinates is $6$, which is not among (A)–(D).

**Answer: (E) another number**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-19.title: Two values of $a$
kangaroo-at-2023-student-19.body:
Take $a = 0$ and $a = 1$: $x^3 + 3x^2 + 4 = x^3 + 3x^2 + x + 6$ gives $x = -2$, and $y = 8$. Sum $6$.

**Answer: (E) another number**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-20.title: Butterfly rule twice
kangaroo-at-2023-student-20.body:
**Fact:** if the diagonals of a quadrilateral cross, the four triangles they form satisfy (product of opposite areas) = (product of the other two opposite areas). Reason: two triangles with a common height have areas in the ratio of their bases, so if the diagonal pieces are $p, q$ and $r, s$, the areas are proportional to $pr, rq, qs, sp$, and $pr\cdot qs = rq\cdot sp$.

Draw the segment from the top vertex to the lower vertex of the grey quadrilateral; it splits $P$ into a left part $u$ and a right part $v$.
- Left quadrilateral (areas 9, 3, 2, $u$ around the crossing point): $9\cdot 2 = 3\cdot u$, so $u = 6$.
- Right quadrilateral (areas 5, 4, 8, $v$): $5\cdot 8 = 4\cdot v$, so $v = 10$.

$P = 6 + 10 = 16$.

**Answer: (C) 16**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-21.title: Odd squares at a corner
kangaroo-at-2023-student-21.body:
In the spiral, $9 = 3^2$ is the upper-left corner of the $3\times3$ block and $25 = 5^2$ the upper-left corner of the $5\times5$ block. After $25$ the spiral continues one step **up** (26) and then turns **right** (27, ...). The same happens after every odd square: the spiral completes the $k\times k$ square at its upper-left corner with $k^2$, goes up one step and turns right.

$625 = 25^2$ is an odd square, so $626$ is directly above $625$ and $627$ is to the right of $626$.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-22.title: Count divisors
kangaroo-at-2023-student-22.body:
$2^{20}\cdot3^{23}$ has $(20+1)(23+1) = 504$ divisors. The divisors of it that also divide $2^{10}\cdot3^{20}$ are exactly the divisors of $2^{10}\cdot3^{20}$: $11\cdot21 = 231$. Answer: $504 - 231 = 273$.

**Answer: (C) 273**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-22.title: Count directly
kangaroo-at-2023-student-22.body:
A divisor $2^i3^j$ ($0\le i\le 20$, $0\le j\le 23$) fails to divide $2^{10}3^{20}$ iff $i > 10$ or $j > 20$. With $i>10$: $10\cdot 24 = 240$; with $i\le10$ and $j>20$: $11\cdot 3 = 33$. Total $273$.

**Answer: (C) 273**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-23.title: Who can beat Hans?
kangaroo-at-2023-student-23.body:
Say Hans won parts 1 and 2 and came $r$-th in part 3, so he has $r \le 13$ points. Every other athlete has ranks $a, b \ge 2$ in parts 1 and 2 and some rank $c\ge1$ in part 3. To be ahead of Hans he needs $abc < r \le 13$, i.e. $abc \le 12$.

**At most two athletes can be ahead.**
- Only one athlete can have $c = 1$.
- An athlete with $c \ge 2$ needs $ab \le 6$, so $(a,b)$ is $(2,2)$, $(2,3)$ or $(3,2)$. Rank 2 in part 1 and rank 2 in part 2 belong to one athlete each, so there could be two such athletes only as $(2,3,c)$ and $(3,2,c')$. But $6c \le 12$ and $6c'\le 12$ force $c = c' = 2$, impossible (no draws). So at most one athlete with $c\ge2$ is ahead.

Together: at most 2 athletes ahead of Hans.

**Two is possible:** Hans $1\cdot1\cdot13 = 13$, Anna $2\cdot3\cdot1 = 6$, Bert $3\cdot2\cdot2 = 12$, and the other ten athletes get ranks $(k, k, k-1)$ for $k = 4,\dots,13$, so they have at least $4\cdot4\cdot3 = 48$ points. Then Hans is 3rd.

**Answer: (B) 3rd**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-24.title: Label the grid points
kangaroo-at-2023-student-24.body:
Number the corners of the tetrahedron 1, 2, 3, 4, with the marked face $123$ lying on START. When the marker rolls over an edge, the two corners of that edge stay where they are and the fourth corner comes down on the new grid point. So every grid point the marker touches gets a fixed corner number, and the numbers follow a simple rule: along every grid line the numbers alternate in pairs — two grid points that are 2 edge lengths apart on a line always get the same number.

The marked face is down exactly on the triangles whose corners are numbered 1, 2, 3. Going through the triangles of the diagram: A, B, C, D and the unlabelled one each have a corner numbered 4. Triangle $E$ is START shifted by exactly two edge lengths to the right, so its corners carry the same numbers 1, 2, 3 as START.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-25.title: Vieta
kangaroo-at-2023-student-25.body:
Let the integer zeros be $r_1,\dots,r_5$ (with multiplicity). By Vieta, $r_1 + \dots + r_5 = 11$ and $r_1r_2r_3r_4r_5 = 7$. Integers whose product is 7 are $\pm1$'s and one $\pm7$. To reach the sum 11 we need $7 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 11$ (any $-1$ or $-7$ would make the sum smaller). So the polynomial is $(x-1)^4(x-7)$, and $(x-1)^4$ is the highest power dividing it.

**Answer: (D) $(x-1)^4$**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-26.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2023-student-26.body:
Let the big square have side $2s$ with centre at the origin, and let the circle have radius $r$. It touches the right side at its midpoint $(s, 0)$, so its centre is $(s - r, 0)$.
- The 8 cm piece of the horizontal midline goes from the left side $(-s, 0)$ to the circle at $(s - 2r, 0)$: $2s - 2r = 8$, so the centre is at $(4, 0)$.
- The 6 cm piece of the vertical midline goes from the top $(0, s)$ to the circle at $(0, s-6)$. This point is on the circle: $4^2 + (s-6)^2 = r^2 = (s-4)^2$.

Expanding: $16 + s^2 - 12s + 36 = s^2 - 8s + 16$, so $4s = 36$, $s = 9$. Side length $2s = 18$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 18 cm**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-26.title: Power of a point
kangaroo-at-2023-student-26.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of the big square and $s$ half its side. The horizontal line through $O$ meets the circle at distance $s - 8$ to the left of $O$ and $s$ to the right of $O$ (at the touching point). The vertical line through $O$ meets the circle at distance $s - 6$ above $O$, and by symmetry (the centre of the circle is on the horizontal line) also $s-6$ below. Intersecting chords through $O$: $(s-8)\cdot s = (s-6)^2$, so $s^2 - 8s = s^2 - 12s + 36$, $s = 9$, side $18$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 18 cm**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-27.title: Five consecutive numbers
kangaroo-at-2023-student-27.body:
The expression is $\big(n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)\big)^3$. The product of 5 consecutive integers is always divisible by $5! = 120$ (it equals $120\binom{n+4}{5}$), and for $n = 1$ it equals 120. So the gcd of all these products is 120, and the gcd of their cubes is $120^3 = 2^9\cdot3^3\cdot5^3$.

(For $n=1$ the expression is $120^3$, so the common factor divides $120^3$; and every value is a multiple of $120^3$.)

**Answer: (E) $2^9\cdot3^3\cdot5^3$**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-28.title: Compare triples with a common hexagon
kangaroo-at-2023-student-28.body:
Name the top row $6, t_2, t_3, ?$, the middle row $m_1, m_2, m_3$ and the bottom row $4, b_2, b_3, 11$. The bold points give the triples $\{6,t_2,m_1\}, \{t_2,t_3,m_2\}, \{t_3,?,m_3\}$ (top) and $\{m_1,4,b_2\}, \{m_2,b_2,b_3\}, \{m_3,b_3,11\}$ (bottom), all with the same sum.

Compare triples that share a middle hexagon:
- via $m_1$: $6 + t_2 = 4 + b_2$, so $b_2 = t_2 + 2$;
- via $m_2$: $t_2 + t_3 = b_2 + b_3$, so $t_3 = b_3 + 2$;
- via $m_3$: $t_3 + {?} = b_3 + 11$, so $? = 11 - 2 = 9$.

(A complete filling exists: top $6, 8, 7, 9$, middle $3, 2, 1$, bottom $4, 10, 5, 11$, all sums 17.)

**Answer: (E) 9**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-29.title: Volume of the slanted water
kangaroo-at-2023-student-29.body:
The radius is $r = \sqrt3$ cm. Let the leaning glass make angle $\theta$ with the vertical. Its bottom is a tilted disc; its lowest point is on the table and its highest point is at height $2r\sin\theta$. The water surface touches the bottom only at this highest point, so the water height is $h = 2r\sin\theta$.

The water in the leaning glass is a cylinder cut obliquely by a plane that does not cut its base. Such a piece has volume (base area) $\times$ (length of the axis inside it). The axis starts at the centre of the bottom, which is $r\sin\theta$ below the water surface, so the axis length inside the water is $\frac{r\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.

Equal volumes: $\pi r^2\cdot 2r\sin\theta = \pi r^2\cdot\frac{r\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, so $\cos\theta = \frac12$, $\theta = 60^\circ$. Then $h = 2\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 3$ cm and the volume is $3\pi\cdot 3 = 9\pi$ cm³.

**Answer: (A) $9\pi$ cm³**

kangaroo-at-2023-student-30.title: Divisibility by 10, 8 and 9
kangaroo-at-2023-student-30.body:
A product of six consecutive integers is divisible by $6! = 720 = 16\cdot9\cdot5$.
- It is divisible by 10, so the last digit $b = 0$. Then $a, c, d$ are $1, 2, 3$ in some order (four consecutive digits containing 0).
- Divisible by 9: the digit sum $2a + 2c + 4d = 2(a+c+d) + 2d = 12 + 2d$ must be a multiple of 9, so $d = 3$.

(Indeed $74\cdot75\cdot76\cdot77\cdot78\cdot79 = 200\,133\,133\,200$.)

**Answer: (C) 3**
